newsitem.title: NORWAY: Holbrooke, Wei front runners for Nobel Peace Prize.
newsitem.headline: Holbrooke, Wei front runners for Nobel Peace Prize.

text.p: Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. architect of Bosnia's peace treaty, is a leading candidate for the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize to be announced on Friday by the Norwegian Nobel Committee, observers say.
Other names mentioned as front runners in Oslo include jailed Chinese dissident Wei Jingsheng and former U.S. president Jimmy Carter.
If the committee decides to reward an organisation, the Salvation Army or medical aid charity Medecins sans Frontieres could win, journalists and observers suggest.

The Nobel Committee, in keeping with its tradition of secrecy, offers little clue to the possible winner. It said some 120 candidates, including 29 organisations, were nominated for the 1996 award, but it has refused to confirm a single name.

The five Nobel Committee members often use the prestigious prize to encourage politicians or activists with unfinished work in a peace or democracy process -- a factor that favours both Holbrooke and Wei.
"They look to the future as well as to the past in making their choice," one diplomat said.
Bosnia held its first post-war election last month, a key stage in the implementation of the 1995 Dayton treaty which Holbrooke's energetic diplomacy did much to broker.

But peace is still considered fragile in Bosnia with ethnic hatred rampant and Holbrooke -- speaking at the Nobel Foundation in Oslo a month ago -- called for a new Dayton-type conference to encourage former enemies to work together.
Nobel officials stressed that Holbrooke's visit as guest speaker was not linked to the $1.12 million prize.
While other leading candidates have been nominated before, Holbrooke, now a Wall Street businesman, is a new name on the list of would-be peace laureates.

"He is seen as a red-hot favourite -- probably in his own mind too," veteran political commentator Svein Rohne wrote in tabloid Verdens Gang. "His office has told the press that although Holbrooke is travelling now, he will be back on Friday -- in case someone wants to speak to him."
"Holbrooke is not a bad guess," said Lars Hellberg, political commentator at Aftenposten, Norway's main newspaper.
But he conceded: "We haven't got a clue."

Nobel Institute Director Geir Lundestad revealed last week the committee had reached a decision. "We cannot have giant surprises like we had last year but we will see," he said enigmatically. "I don't want to say anything more."
Nobel watchers were caught on the hop last year when the award went to little-known veteran anti-nuclear campaigner Joseph Rotblat and his Pugwash organisation.
China's Wei, regarded as the father of the Communist state's tiny and embattled democracy movement, came to the fore last February when the Nobel Committee shrugged off a Chinese condemnation of him.
The committee said it would not give in to pressure in selecting laureates.

Carter, who was president from 1977 to 1981, is recognised worldwide for his peacemaking and humanitarian efforts in Africa, Asia and the Caribbean. But the fact that he has been nominated at least five times before could weaken his candidacy.

The prize, first awarded in 1901, is named after Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel. He had thought his invention of dynamite would end all wars by acting as the ultimate deterrent but to be sure endowed the peace prize in his will.
